Why behaviour changes: Baristas prioritize time efficiency and space savings in small homes or offices; a compact machine reduces setup time and footprint.. How value is captured: Premium pricing justified by convenience; Simonelli can capture value through direct-to-consumer sales and brand positioning as a home convenience leader.. Assumptions: Home barista market exists and is willing to pay for convenience.; Simonelli can produce a compact machine without compromising performance.; Marketing can effectively communicate convenience benefits.. Why behaviour changes: The rise of home barista culture, driven by social media and the desire for a third-place coffee experience, creates demand for equipment that is easy to use and produces consistent results.. T2: Consumers are increasingly seeking convenience and ease of use in coffee equipment, leading them to prefer machines that require minimal skill and maintenance. Who benefits: Time-constrained consumers who want quick, high-quality coffee without the hassle of manual brewing.. Why behaviour changes: The demand for convenience grows as people juggle busy schedules and seek quick solutions for daily coffee needs.. How value is captured: Simonelli can capture value by offering consumer machines with simplified operation, automatic features, and low maintenance, allowing premium pricing and reduced customer support costs.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience over manual control.; Automatic and simplified machines are perceived as more desirable.; Simonelli can differentiate its consumer offerings with ease-of-use features.. Predictions: A survey of consumers will show a growing preference for machines with automatic brewing and minimal manual intervention.; Sales of Simonelli's consumer offerings will increase in regions where convenience is a key purchase criterion.; Customers will report higher satisfaction with ease of use compared to competitors..

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

T1: Home baristas value social interaction and community, and will purchase equipment that enables sharing experiences, leading to demand for consumer-oriented features. Who benefits: Simonelli Group would benefit by capturing premium pricing for social-friendly features and expanding its consumer base beyond professional buyers.. Why behaviour changes: The pandemic highlighted the importance of social interaction in coffee culture, creating a desire for equipment that facilitates sharing and community.. How value is captured: Simonelli can charge higher prices for social features and expand its consumer market by positioning equipment as a social hub rather than just a machine.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize social experience over technical performance in home espresso equipment.; Simonelli can design or adapt equipment to support shared use (e.g., multiple cups, display, or social media integration).; There is a willing consumer segment willing to pay a premium for social-friendly features.. Predictions: If offered a social-friendly feature, consumer surveys will show higher purchase intent than a featureless machine.; Sales of a social-friendly model will exceed sales of a standard professional model in the same segment.; Simonelli will see higher average transaction value when selling to consumers with social features..

T2: Consumers value convenience and ease of use, and will purchase equipment that simplifies preparation, leading to demand for consumer-oriented features. Who benefits: Simonelli Group would benefit by capturing higher margins on simplified models and expanding its consumer base through lower entry barriers.. Why behaviour changes: Post-pandemic, consumers seek products that reduce time and effort, especially for home use. Simplified controls and compact designs address this need.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price consumer models at a premium for convenience features and sell through retail channels, increasing overall revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience over technical performance for home espresso equipment.; Simonelli can design or adapt equipment to feature simplified controls and compact form factors.; There is a willing consumer segment willing to pay a premium for convenience.. Predictions: If offered a simplified model, consumer surveys will show higher purchase intent than a standard professional model.; Sales of a simplified model will exceed sales of a standard professional model in the same segment.; Simonelli will see higher average transaction value when selling to consumers with simplified features..

Randomly split each segment into two halves (250 each) to test both segments.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each segment and for each product variant. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electrony's Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.. Constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.; Must consider competitive landscape, regulatory barriers, and current consumer reach of Electrony's products.; Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or a clear value capture mechanism.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a niche segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add‑on accessories, subscription services).; 3) Maintain the current professional focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).; 4) Partner with or license Electrony's technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than creating a direct consumer product..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, long‑life appliance that reduces future repair and replacement costs. Who benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners who currently replace appliances frequently.. Why behaviour changes: A willingness to pay a 10% premium for a product advertised to last longer and have a longer warranty creates a perceived cost‑savings mechanism that motivates purchase.. How value is captured: Electrolux can charge a premium price for the differentiated line and capture higher margins through brand differentiation and reduced service calls.. Assumptions: Consumers are price‑sensitive and value long‑term reliability.; Electrolux can communicate the durability claim effectively to consumers.; The premium price is acceptable to a segment of consumers willing to pay extra for quality.. Predictions: In a survey, consumers will indicate they would pay at least 10% more for a product advertised with a longer commercial guarantee.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed as a premium, long‑life appliance compared to a standard model.; Sales of the differentiated line will be driven by consumers who already own professional‑grade appliances and seek home‑grade reliability..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it offers a self‑service, resource‑efficient solution that reduces operational costs and improves uptime, especially in small businesses and multi‑family housing. Who benefits: Small‑business owners and property managers who need reliable, low‑maintenance laundry equipment.. Why behaviour changes: A willingness to pay for a self‑service system that minimizes downtime and labor costs creates a functional incentive to adopt the product.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell integrated self‑service units at a premium, capture recurring service and maintenance revenue, and differentiate through resource‑efficiency claims.. Assumptions: Small‑business owners prioritize operational efficiency and cost savings.; Self‑service formats are feasible and acceptable to consumers in residential settings.; Electrolux can deliver the performance required for a self‑service solution.. Predictions: In a test, small‑business owners will show higher purchase intent for a self‑service unit compared to a standard unit.; The unit will achieve higher uptime and lower maintenance frequency in pilot deployments.; Sales will be driven by businesses that already use professional‑grade equipment and seek home‑grade reliability..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home vs. Business Segment" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 2,000 respondents: 1,000 U.S. homeowners (self‑reported need for home laundry reliability) and 1,000 small‑business owners (self‑reported need for operational efficiency).. Measure: Average WTP in euros for a differentiated line (e.g., a compact, long‑life washing machine) and a self‑service unit (e.g., a modular, low‑maintenance unit).. Predictions: T1: Home segment WTP ≥ €1,200 (10% premium) and self‑service unit WTP ≤ €1,200.; T2: Small‑business segment WTP ≥ €1,200 and self‑service unit WTP ≥ €1,200.. Decision rule: If home segment WTP ≥ €1,200 AND self‑service unit WTP ≥ €1,200, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners with a premium, long‑life line. If small‑business segment WTP ≥ €1,200 AND self‑service unit WTP. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners who value long‑life reliability, supported by evidence that consumers are willing to pay a 10% premium for durable appliances. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and price sensitivity before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of durability and repairability versus performance and price descriptions among a recruited population of household washing-machine buyers. It does not address consumer willingness to pay a premium for long‑life durability, so it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners who value long‑life reliability, supported by evidence that consumers are willing to pay a 10% premium for durable appliances. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and price sensitivity before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and small‑business owners who currently replace appliances frequently and seek reliable, long‑term performance.. Value proposition: A compact, long‑life washing machine marketed with a durability and repairability claim, offering a 10% premium price and reduced future repair and replacement costs.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey (2,000 respondents, €15,000, 8 weeks) to validate demand and price sensitivity before committing to product development.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay a 10% premium for a durable appliance is uncertain; the pilot will determine whether consumers will convert interest into purchases.. Would change if: If the survey shows home segment WTP below €1,200 or small‑business segment WTP below €1,200, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of a different consumer proposition or no expansion.; If new evidence shows strong demand for self‑service functionality among small‑business owners, the recommendation would shift toward a self‑service consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.. Assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.; A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.; Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.; Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, low‑maintenance solution that reduces the hassle of bottled water or other alternative water sources. Who benefits: Busy households and consumers who currently spend time and money on bottled water, delivery services, or other water alternatives.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin offers a membrane that is easy to install, requires minimal maintenance (e.g., cartridge replacement indicator), and integrates with smart home systems, consumers will switch from the hassle of bottled water to a single, self‑s. How value is captured: Lower upfront cost compared to premium membrane, subscription services for maintenance, and data‑driven insights that enhance convenience through smart home integration.. Assumptions: Consumers currently find bottled water delivery inconvenient or expensive.; A low‑maintenance membrane reduces perceived effort.; Smart home compatibility can be marketed as a convenience benefit.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher repeat purchase rates than standard membranes.; Pilot units will achieve higher adoption rates in households with children or elderly members..

Test "Messaging Test: Premium vs Convenience Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with between‑subjects design. Participants view two versions of a product description (premium vs convenience) for the same membrane. They select which version they would purchase and indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and perceived importance of attributes (taste, safety, convenience, maintenance).. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a representative Danish population.. Measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent (binary: would purchase premium vs convenience version). Secondary outcomes: WTP (max price participants would pay) and importance ratings (1‑10).. Predictions: T1: Premium messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher WTP than convenience messaging, because health‑enhancing positioning aligns with T1’s claim that premium perception drives adoption.; T2: Convenience messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher WTP than premium messaging, because low‑maintenance positioning aligns with T2’s claim that convenience reduces perceived effort and drives adoption.. Decision rule: If premium messaging achieves at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent than convenience messaging, and the difference in WTP is at least €10, then T1 is supported and a differentiated premium consumer proposition is justified.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience, particularly in Denmark and potentially other markets where tap water quality is perceived as uncertain.. Value proposition: A high‑performance membrane that eliminates taste concerns, provides clear health benefits, and offers easy installation and low maintenance, enabling premium pricing and subscription services for maintenance.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed messaging test (500 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare premium vs. convenience messaging and determine whether premium positioning drives higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium‑willing segment, actual willingness to pay, and the ability to scale production and distribution remain uncertain. Evidence of strong demand for a differentiated proposition is needed before committing resources.. Would change if: If the messaging test shows convenience messaging achieving at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent and a €10 price premium, or if a survey reveals that taste/safety is the primary barrier to tap water use, we would shift focus; to a convenience‑focused proposition and explore low‑upfront‑cost models.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive water quality as a health risk and trust the membrane technology, leading to higher willingness to pay for a branded home water filter. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or public tap water they distrust.. Why behaviour changes: Negative perceptions of tap water quality and safety (as shown in Flanders study) create a perceived health risk that motivates purchase of a membrane-based purifier.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can charge a premium price for a branded consumer unit and capture value through direct-to-consumer sales and repeat cartridge/filter sales.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to switch from bottled water to a membrane-based alternative if they trust the technology; Health concerns outweigh price sensitivity for a segment of consumers; Aquaporin can communicate the health benefit effectively to reach this segment. Predictions: In a survey of health-conscious consumers, at least 30% will state they would purchase a membrane-based home water filter if priced at €200-€300; Purchase intent will be higher in regions with high bottled water consumption and low trust in tap water quality.

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive water quality as a convenience and trust the membrane technology, leading to higher willingness to pay for a branded home water filter. Who benefits: Time-poor households that currently rely on bottled water or public tap water they trust for convenience.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience and trust in the membrane technology reduce the perceived effort of water procurement, making a branded home filter attractive even at a premium price.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value through premium-priced direct-to-consumer units and recurring cartridge/filter sales, leveraging its membrane technology as a convenience product.. Assumptions: Convenience and trust outweigh health concerns for a segment of consumers; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that simplifies water procurement; Aquaporin can effectively communicate convenience benefits to reach this segment. Predictions: In a survey of time-poor consumers, at least 25% will state they would purchase a membrane-based home water filter if priced at €250-€350; Purchase intent will be higher in regions with high bottled water consumption and low trust in tap water quality.

Test "Segmented purchase intent survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a health-focused message (perceived water quality risk) or a convenience-focused message (time-saving benefit). Participants are recruited from two segments: health-conscious consumers (n=300) and time-poor consumers (n=300). Both segments see the same product description and price point (proposed €250-€350).. Sample: 300 health-conscious consumers and 300 time-poor consumers, recruited via targeted online panels to match demographic distribution of target markets.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Health-conscious segment will show higher average purchase intent and WTP than time-poor segment, with a difference of at least 1.5 points on the intent scale.; T2: Time-poor segment will show higher average purchase intent and WTP than health-conscious segment, with a difference of at least 1.5 points on the intent scale.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent of the health-conscious segment is at least 1.5 points higher than the time-poor segment, proceed with a differentiated health-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite difference is observed, proceed with. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health-conscious consumers who distrust tap water quality. Begin with a limited pilot of a branded home water filter positioned on health benefits, using the proposed segmented purchase intent survey to validate demand before full-scale rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test (SYN-AQP-UPDATE) does not address consumer motivation (health vs convenience) and therefore does not affect T1. The evidence it bears on is neutral, as it measures maintenance-plan enrollment, not membrane efficacy, health concerns, or consumer willingness to pay. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-AQP-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health-conscious consumers who distrust tap water quality. Begin with a limited pilot of a branded home water filter positioned on health benefits, using the proposed segmented purchase intent survey to validate demand before full-scale rollout. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers in markets where tap water quality is perceived as unsafe or unhealthy, currently relying on bottled water.. Value proposition: A membrane-based home water filter that communicates proven water quality and safety, offering a premium-priced branded unit with recurring cartridge sales to capture recurring revenue.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 10-week, €18,000 segmented purchase intent survey to compare health-focused and convenience-focused messaging, and use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a pilot.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay and purchase intent for a health-focused proposition are unknown; the pilot will resolve this. Also uncertain is the competitive response from established consumer brands and the ability to communicate health. Would change if: If the survey shows the time-poor segment has at least 1.5 points higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the health segment, we would shift focus to a convenience-driven proposition.; If a competitor launches a successful health-focused consumer brand at a similar price point, we would reconsider the positioning and pricing strategy.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, long‑life product that offers superior durability and commercial‑grade performance, and are willing to pay a premium for it. Who benefits: Electrolux Professional Group captures higher margin sales and brand prestige by entering the consumer market with a differentiated offering.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently treat household appliances as disposable; a product positioned as a long‑life, commercial‑grade appliance signals durability and reliability, prompting them to choose it over cheaper alternatives.. How value is captured: Electrolux can charge premium prices for the differentiated product, sell through retail and wholesale channels, and potentially expand into subscription or service models for extended warranty or maintenance.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of and value commercial‑grade durability.; The premium price is acceptable to a segment of consumers willing to pay extra for long‑life products.; Retail and wholesale channels can effectively reach the target consumer segment.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated consumer product at a 10% premium price, at least 20% of surveyed consumers will express intent to purchase or place a pre‑order within 12 weeks.; Sales of the differentiated product will generate higher average revenue per unit compared to a baseline product at the same price point..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it is marketed as a convenient, self‑service solution that reduces the need for manual laundry management, and are willing to pay for the convenience. Who benefits: Electrolux Professional Group captures higher margin sales by selling a self‑service unit directly to consumers or through retail channels, and can potentially expand into subscription or service models.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers in multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other spaces face time‑constrained schedules and lack access to laundry facilities; a self‑service unit removes the need to visit a laundromat, making laundry more convenient and atr. How value is captured: Electrolux can price the unit at a premium for convenience, sell through retail and wholesale channels, and generate recurring revenue from optional accessories or extended warranty services.. Assumptions: Consumers perceive self‑service laundry as a time‑saving convenience.; The convenience value is sufficient to justify a premium price over traditional laundry methods.; Retail and wholesale channels can effectively reach the target consumer segment.. Predictions: In a test offering a self‑service consumer unit at a 10% premium price, at least 20% of surveyed consumers will express intent to purchase or place a pre‑order within 12 weeks.; Sales of the self‑service unit will generate higher average revenue per unit compared to a baseline unit at the same price point..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Premium Durability vs Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to one of two product concepts and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. Participants view a product description of a self‑service consumer unit (T2) or a differentiated consumer unit (T1) positioned as a long‑life, commercial‑grade appliance (T1). They are then asked: "How much would you pay a 10% premium over a standard unit for this product?". Sample: 500 adult consumers in the United Kingdom, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income. Stratify by household size to test both concepts.. Measure: Percentage of respondents who state a WTP of at least £100 (or equivalent currency) for the product, and average WTP amount.. Predictions: T1: At least 20% of respondents will state a WTP of at least £100 for the differentiated product, indicating demand for premium durability.; T2: At least 20% of respondents will state a WTP of at least £100 for the self‑service unit, indicating demand for convenience.. Decision rule: If the observed WTP for the differentiated product (T1) is at least 20% and exceeds the WTP for the self‑service unit (T2), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium durability. If the opposite is true, do. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a long‑life, commercial‑grade appliance offering premium durability and reliability. Begin with a limited pilot in retail and wholesale channels to test consumer willingness to pay a premium. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a long‑life, commercial‑grade appliance offering premium durability and reliability. Begin with a limited pilot in retail and wholesale channels to test consumer willingness to pay a premium. Target customer: Residential consumers in multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other spaces where self‑service laundry is feasible and demand for commercial‑quality home appliances is growing.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer unit that delivers superior durability, commercial‑grade performance, and a longer warranty, allowing consumers to choose a long‑life appliance over cheaper, disposable alternatives.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (500 UK adults, randomized exposure to premium durability vs convenience concepts, WTP threshold of €100). Use results to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.. Uncertainty: The willingness to pay a premium for durability is uncertain; evidence shows consumers are willing to pay extra for long‑life products (T1), but no source directly measures premium price acceptance. Convenience demand (T2) is also uncertain. Would change if: If the test shows the self‑service unit (T2) achieving at least 20% WTP at €100 or higher, indicating stronger convenience demand, we would shift focus to a self‑service consumer unit.; If no test data is available or the results are below the 20% threshold, we would maintain the current professional focus and not pursue consumer expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

Test "Membrane Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Sample: 500 Danish adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a differentiated membrane (premium taste/health vs. low‑maintenance convenience) and self‑reported primary reason for choosing the membrane.. Predictions: T1: Group receiving premium positioning will show WTP at least 20% higher than the low‑maintenance group, and will cite taste or health concerns as primary reason.; T2: Group receiving low‑maintenance positioning will show WTP at least 20% higher than the premium group, and will cite convenience or reduced effort as primary reason.. Decision rule: If premium group WTP ≥ 20% of low‑maintenance group WTP AND taste/health is cited by ≥ 60% of premium group, proceed to develop a differentiated premium proposition. If low‑maintenance WTP ≥ 20% of premium group AND convenience is cited by. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
T1 kept: Simulated warehouse test SYN-D concerns packing errors and does not address consumer perception of premium taste/health benefits, so it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience, particularly in Denmark and potentially other markets where tap water quality is perceived as uncertain.. Value proposition: A differentiated membrane that delivers superior taste, clear health benefits, and easy installation/maintenance, positioned as a premium home purifier that reduces reliance on bottled water.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Membrane Preference Test (500 Danish adults, three groups, willingness to pay and primary reason for choosing). Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a premium positioning pilot.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium‑positioning premium over low‑maintenance convenience is unknown; consumer willingness to pay for taste/health benefits is not quantified; market size for a differentiated unit is uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows low‑maintenance convenience WTP at least 20% higher than premium taste/health WTP, or if a survey reveals convenience as the primary reason for choosing a membrane, we would shift focus to a low‑maintenance proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers who want to avoid contaminants and are willing to pay more for a product they believe is safe.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing tap water as unsafe to viewing a membrane purifier as a safe, effective alternative, they will purchase it even if the price is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling it directly to consumers through online channels and retail partners, and leveraging the brand reputation for safety.. Assumptions: Consumers trust membrane technology more than bottled water.; Health concerns are a primary purchase driver for a significant segment of the market.; Price sensitivity is lower for a premium health product than for a standard consumer product.. Predictions: Surveyed health-conscious consumers will indicate higher willingness to pay for a membrane purifier compared to a standard filter.; Sales of the differentiated product will be concentrated among households with children, elderly, or those with known water quality concerns.; Competitor products will not achieve similar premium pricing due to lower perceived safety..

Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purification as a chore to viewing it as a seamless, automatic process, they will choose a product that requires minimal maintenance and installation.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the differentiated product as a plug-and-play solution, offering subscription-based cartridge replacements and direct-to-consumer online sales, and leveraging the brand for convenience.. Assumptions: Maintenance frequency is a significant purchase barrier for consumers.; Convenience and ease of use are more important than price for a segment of the market.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that saves time.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, long‑life product that aligns with their growing demand for durable, commercial‑grade home appliances. Who benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners seeking reliable, high‑performance laundry solutions that reduce replacement frequency.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently treat home appliances as disposable; a premium, longer‑warranty product signals durability and lower long‑term cost, prompting them to choose a single premium machine over multiple cheaper units.. How value is captured: Electrolux can charge a premium price for a differentiated unit, capture higher margins, and build brand loyalty by positioning the product as a premium, long‑life solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a 10‑15% premium for a product advertised as lasting longer.; The premium is communicated effectively through marketing and warranty messaging.; Distribution channels can reach the target segment without significant cost increase.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated unit, purchase intent among homeowners will be at least 20% higher than for a standard unit at a comparable price.; Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 10% more for a product advertised with a longer commercial guarantee..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it offers a self‑service, resource‑efficient solution that reduces operational costs and downtime, particularly for small businesses and multi‑family housing. Who benefits: Small business owners and property managers seeking lower labor and energy costs, and residents in multi‑family buildings looking to reduce wait times and maintenance.. Why behaviour changes: Self‑service machines eliminate the need for staff, reducing labor costs and downtime, while their compact design fits small spaces. This cost‑of‑ownership advantage makes the product attractive even at a comparable price.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell a self‑service unit at a premium, capture higher margins, and build a subscription or service‑model revenue stream by offering maintenance and consumables.. Assumptions: Small businesses and multi‑family housing are willing to pay a premium for a unit that reduces labor and energy costs.; The unit's compact design and self‑service features are feasible and do not compromise performance.; Distribution and service logistics can be managed within the test budget.. Predictions: In a test offering a self‑service unit, small business owners will report at least 15% lower monthly operational costs compared to a standard unit.; Residents in multi‑family buildings will indicate willingness to pay at least 10% more for a unit that reduces wait times and maintenance..

Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Premium condition will have at least 20% higher purchase intent and WTP than self‑service condition.; T2: Self‑service condition will have at least 20% higher purchase intent and WTP than premium condition.. Decision rule: If premium condition exceeds self‑service condition by ≥20% in both purchase intent and WTP, proceed with premium differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Simonelli Group would benefit by capturing higher-margin consumer sales and building brand loyalty among home barista enthusiasts.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers seek more than functional coffee; they want to engage in a social activity and express personal style, making them willing to invest in equipment that reflects their identity and community.. How value is captured: Simonelli can charge premium prices for differentiated models, sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, and leverage storytelling around the home barista experience to justify higher margins.. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offers for two Simonelli machine concepts: (1) a differentiated home barista model emphasizing social ritual and identity (e.g., "Create your own third place coffee experience"), and (2) a convenience-focused model emphasizing quick, easy prep for busy lifestyles (e.g., "Espresso in 30 seconds, no expertise needed"). Participants view each concept and indicate willingness to pay.. Sample: 300 U.S. adults who have expressed interest in home coffee equipment (recruited via panels), balanced for age, gender, and self-reported coffee consumption frequency.. Measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 1‑10 scale for each concept, and self-reported importance of social ritual vs. convenience as a purchase criterion.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP for the differentiated concept (social ritual) and higher proportion of participants citing social ritual as the primary purchase reason.; T2: Higher average WTP for the convenience concept (quick prep) and higher proportion of participants citing convenience as the primary purchase reason.. Group B sees a home coffee machine (simplified, easy-to-use machine) and is asked to indicate willingness to pay a premium price. Both groups are asked the same price point and a. Sample: 300 adult consumers aged 25-55 who have purchased coffee equipment in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel. Stratified by region to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for each product, measured as the maximum price participants would pay. Secondary measure: stated intent to purchase on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show a significantly higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, indicating demand for a home barista machine.; T2: Group B will show a significantly higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, indicating demand for a home coffee machine.. Decision rule: If the difference in average WTP between the two groups is at least €20 (a threshold derived from a pilot test showing a €15 difference is a meaningful purchase decision), we conclude that the product aligned with the theory (T1 or T2) is. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Home Barista vs. Speed-Conc" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Measure: 1) WTP for a Simonelli home barista machine (e.g., price and features). 2) WTP for a Simonelli speed/large‑water‑tank machine (e.g., price and features). 3) Secondary measure: stated importance of social interaction vs. speed.. Predictions: T1: Home baristas show higher WTP for the home barista machine and higher importance of social interaction than time‑constrained consumers.; T2: Time‑constrained consumers show higher WTP for the speed/large‑water‑tank machine and higher importance of speed than home baristas.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the home barista machine exceeds the WTP for the speed machine by at least 15 percentage points among home baristas, proceed to develop a differentiated home barista proposition. Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product launch. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) premium, home-barista focus (emphasizing quality, social experience, and personal enjoyment) or (B) professional, shop-focused (emphasizing brand prestige, professional standards, and shop compatibility). Participants view a product description of a new consumer espresso machine (e.g., compact, easy. Sample: 400 participants: 200 assigned to Condition A, 200 assigned to Condition B. Recruit via coffee enthusiast panels and social media to ensure diversity in age, gender, and coffee consumption habits.. Measure: Primary measure: average stated willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. Secondary measures: purchase intent (binary: would buy), brand perception (Likert scale), and intent to recommend to peers.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition A (home-barista messaging) than in Condition B.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition B (professional messaging) than in Condition A.. Decision rule: If the difference in average WTP between the two conditions is at least €20 (indicating Condition A is significantly more willing to pay) and the purchase intent difference is at least 15 percentage points in favor of Condition A, proceed. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home barista enthusiasts, leveraging premium positioning and direct-to-consumer channels. Begin with a limited launch of a compact, high-quality espresso machine and build brand awareness through specialty retailers and social media. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home barista enthusiasts, leveraging premium positioning and direct-to-consumer channels. Begin with a limited launch of a compact, high-quality espresso machine and build brand awareness through specialty retailers and social media. Target customer: Home barista enthusiasts who enjoy coffee at home for social and personal enjoyment, and who value quality and brand.. Value proposition: A premium, compact espresso machine that combines professional performance with a user-friendly design, positioned as the ultimate home barista tool for personal enjoyment and social sharing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full product launch.. Uncertainty: The long-term sustainability of home barista culture and consumer willingness to pay a premium for espresso equipment remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.. Would change if: If the test shows no significant difference in willingness to pay between the two messaging conditions, or if purchase intent is low, the recommendation would shift toward expanding the professional line or maintaining the current portfolio; If new evidence shows a strong decline in home barista culture or consumer demand for premium equipment, the recommendation would shift toward a different strategy. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Electrolux Professional Group should develop a differentiated consumer proposition beyond its existing professional laundry offering, and if so, what specific use case and evidence would justify this investment.. Constraints: No expansion into consumer markets beyond professional laundry.; Test budget of 20,000 euros and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions.; No access to confidential financial or contractual details.. Alternatives: No expansion: Continue focusing on professional laundry equipment, avoiding consumer markets to maintain existing customer relationships and operational efficiency.; Consumer laundry expansion: Develop a differentiated proposition targeting individual consumers, such as home laundry solutions, potentially leveraging existing professional equipment for consumer use.; Niche professional market expansion: Focus on a specific, underserved professional market (e.g., small hotels, boutique laundries) with a unique value proposition..

T1: Electrolux Professional Group should develop a differentiated consumer proposition for self-service laundry solutions to capture premium pricing and expand its addressable market. Who benefits: Electrolux Professional Group (through higher revenue from consumer sales and expanded customer base).. Why behaviour changes: Individuals and organizations increasingly value convenience, cost-effectiveness, and control over laundry services, driving demand for self-service solutions.. How value is captured: Premium pricing on self-service machines, increased market share, and diversification of revenue streams.. Assumptions: Consumer demand for self-service laundry solutions is growing.; Electrolux Professional Group can effectively market and sell these solutions to individual buyers.; Competitors are not strongly positioned in this market segment.. Predictions: Increased sales of self-service laundry machines to individual buyers.; Higher revenue from consumer sales.; Expanded addressable market beyond professional laundry..
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).
